{"id": "20:70/q20", "question": "What inward change accompanied their prostration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:70/q20/p1", "position": "Divine illumination and devotion drew them from ego and imitation to inward sight, sincere faith, and prostration of the heart.", "reasons": "Qushayri describes inward suns of gnosis and lights of divine care, through which they saw God inwardly. Bursevi transmits a Sufi authority that devotion removes ego's claims and brings sincerity, certainty, and divine lights; the magicians believed by proof, while Pharaoh saw no proof of his claimed lordship. Alusi says their swift guidance shows that recent penitents can attain spiritual perfection and arrival to God."}]}
{"id": "20:70/q21", "question": "What does their defeat teach about miracles, saintly gifts, and sorcery?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:70/q21/p1", "position": "A prophet's miracle or saint's gift draws on higher divine orientation, whereas sorcery weakens through attachment to nature.", "reasons": "Qashani says extraordinary acts can arise through material combinations, prepared images attracting celestial forces, or soul-power; a prophetic miracle comes with challenge and opposition, unlike a non-prophet saint's gift. He says the sorcerer may first exert strong influence but then weakens by turning from the higher source, while prophet or saint strengthens; a defeated sorcerer often accepts the prophet unless natural inclination has erased his capacity."}]}
{"id": "20:70/q22", "question": "Does their naming Aaron and Moses imply that knowledge of God comes only through an Imam?", "turns_on": "Whether their naming of Aaron and Moses establishes a necessary route to knowledge of God.", "positions": [{"id": "20:70/q22/p1", "position": "Yes; the naming of Aaron and Moses indicates that knowledge of God comes only through an Imam.", "reasons": "Razi reports this inference from the Ta'limiyya."}, {"id": "20:70/q22/p2", "position": "No; that inference is weak, and their wording has other benefits.", "reasons": "Razi rejects the Ta'limiyya's inference and says the wording serves other benefits."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q01", "question": "Who speaks in this verse, and to whom?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q01/p1", "position": "Pharaoh speaks to the believing magicians.", "reasons": "Yahyā identifies Pharaoh as speaker; Muqātil identifies the magicians as those addressed; Ṭabarī's report from Wahb places the outburst after their belief and Pharaoh's defeat."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q02", "question": "How is ءَامَنتُمْ read?", "turns_on": "Whether an interrogative hamza is supplied, and how the second hamza is transmitted or eased; both sentence forms can express Pharaoh's rebuke.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q02/p1", "position": "As a declarative, without an interrogative hamza.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid calls the unlengthened form established for Ḥafṣ and also records Ibn Kathīr and Warsh. Fārisī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya give the same three; Bayḍāwī names Qunbul and Ḥafṣ. Ibn al-Jazarī distinguishes Ruways and al-Aṣbahānī from Warsh, a solitary report through al-Khuzāʿī against other Azraq routes, and divergent reports for Qunbul. Ibn ʿĀshūr gives the later route distribution. Fārisī, Bursawī, Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Ālūsī say the declarative still rebukes."}, {"id": "20:71/q02/p2", "position": "As an interrogative with one hamza followed by a lengthened vowel.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī name Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Ibn ʿĀmir, while Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies Qālūn, Warsh via al-Azraq, Abū Jaʿfar and Rawḥ too. Fārisī says Abū ʿAmr avoids his usual inserted alif between hamzas because of the crowded interrogative hamza, pattern hamza and root alif. The interrogative censures the magicians as effectively as the statement."}, {"id": "20:71/q02/p3", "position": "As an interrogative with two hamzas, the second lengthened or realized.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ibn al-Jawzī name Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim; Ibn ʿĀshūr adds Khalaf. Fārisī notes that Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī keep their regular form. Ibn al-Jazarī gives further routes for Warsh and Hishām and distinguishes Hishām's fully realized from intermediate hamza; Qirāʾāt ER notes easing the second hamza by tashīl without losing the question."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q03", "question": "Which letter is extra in the written forms of ءَامَنتُمْ?", "turns_on": "Whether the waw itself is superfluous or represents a hamza whose eased pronunciation the extra alif signals.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q03/p1", "position": "The alif is extra, and the waw represents the hamza to signal easing in connected recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī argues against al-Dānī's analysis of several spellings."}, {"id": "20:71/q03/p2", "position": "The waw is extra.", "reasons": "This is al-Dānī's view as reported and rejected by Ibn al-Jazarī."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q04", "question": "Who does لَهُۥ refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun follows the immediately mentioned Moses or is understood of his Lord by the parallel wording and the substance of the magicians' faith.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q04/p1", "position": "Moses.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Naḥḥās, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Asad identify Moses; Ālūsī calls him the apparent referent. Ibn ʿĀshūr says both pronouns in the statement refer to Moses. The al-Aʿrāf parallel has bihi, whose referent Abū Ḥayyān says could be Moses or God."}, {"id": "20:71/q04/p2", "position": "God, believed in through Moses or because of his signs.", "reasons": "Al-Baḥr al-ʿUlūm takes the pronoun as their Lord and compares 7:123. Biqāʿī describes belief in God through following or affirming Moses. Ālūsī reports both a direct divine referent and a causal lām analysis, but calls the direct referent discontinuous."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q05", "question": "What does belief with لَـ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the lām conveys simple assent, allegiance or following, a typical human object of belief, or cause through Moses.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q05/p1", "position": "It means believing or affirming Moses; Arabic uses both āmana lahu and āmana bihi.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī and Abū Ḥayyān compare 10:83, 17:90 or 2:55, 12:17, 29:26 and the parallel 7:123; Qurtubī cites Lot at 29:26. Ṭabrisī distinguishes belief as the opposite of disbelief with bāʾ from assent to a person with lām. Jishumī says īmān lexically means assent, while religious usage names specified acts."}, {"id": "20:71/q05/p2", "position": "The lām adds following, submission or allegiance to the person believed.", "reasons": "Jishumī contrasts following with mere belief using bāʾ. Bayḍāwī and Bursawī say the verb incorporates following; Ālūsī derives the force from submission, inqāda lahu, but rejects a derivation from ittabaʿa lahu because ittabaʿa takes a direct object. Ibn ʿĀshūr says lām implies faith arising for his sake, while bāʾ gives cause."}, {"id": "20:71/q05/p3", "position": "The lām commonly marks belief in a human, while bāʾ commonly marks belief in God.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī, Abū Ḥayyān and Ālūsī's report from al-Baḥr cite Quranic examples; Kashshāf cites 9:61. Abū Ḥayyān notes that the parallel 7:123 uses bihi and its pronoun may denote Moses or God; Wāḥidī says the parallel has the same meaning. Abū Ḥayyān adduces 9:61, which distinguishes belief in God from believing the believers, as Qur'anic evidence for lām with a person other than God."}, {"id": "20:71/q05/p4", "position": "The lām is causal: they believed in God because of Moses and the signs.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this analysis; Ibn ʿĀshūr distinguishes faith arising for someone's sake from faith arising because of someone."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q06", "question": "What is Pharaoh's charge in قَبْلَ أَنْ ءَاذَنَ لَكُمْ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q06/p1", "position": "They believed and acted before Pharaoh authorized them.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn Kathīr say they affirmed Moses before any order or leave; Yaḥyā stresses that they had already done it. Qurtubī calls it a rebuke for transgression. Ṭabrisī says Pharaoh foolishly imagined belief required his authorization. Ibn ʿĀshūr says he made unauthorized belief into a punishable insolence after losing the debate; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says his claim of sovereignty made him demand that recognition of truth await his leave."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q07", "question": "Does 'before I permit you' imply he might permit belief later?", "turns_on": "Whether 'before' carries a tactical promise of later leave or only marks that no leave had been granted.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q07/p1", "position": "Pharaoh insinuates that later permission was possible, using hope as well as fear to restrain the crowd.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says stressing 'before' keeps onlookers from following; Ibn ʿĀshūr says Pharaoh claimed he would have allowed belief to make the audience doubt the apparent miracle."}, {"id": "20:71/q07/p2", "position": "No later permission is implied or expected; the point is simply that they acted without it.", "reasons": "Bursawī and Ālūsī deny this inference, with 18:109 cited in the discussion."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q08", "question": "What is an idhn, and how does it differ from an order?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q08/p1", "position": "Permission is notification or release to act, without necessarily willing or obliging the action; an order entails the commander's will.", "reasons": "Jishumī gives the original sense of notification; Ṭabrisī contrasts the permission 'hunt' at 5:2 with the order to establish prayer at 6:72; Ālūsī reports Ṭabrisī's distinction. Bursawī calls permission informing another that an act is approved; Ibn ʿĀshūr glosses adhina lahu as authorizing it."}]}

{"id": "20:71/q10", "question": "Why did Pharaoh say Moses taught the magicians magic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q10/p1", "position": "He fabricated prior training and collusion to explain away their defeat and conversion and keep the public from following them.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī's People of Meanings and Ṭabrisī say the chief story turns the crowd away; Rāzī calls the pupils' feigned defeat a second insinuation after his claim that instantaneous belief lacked reflection. {"id": "20:71/q11", "question": "How are the threats to cut and crucify read?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted verb forms have simple or intensive consonants, and whether intensity stresses repetition, manner, or force.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q11/p1", "position": "With lighter forms of both verbs, from simple cutting and crucifying.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Rāzī report an unnamed reading; Qurtubī assigns it to Ibn Muḥayṣin here and in al-Aʿrāf, with open hamza and lighter doubling; Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī also record it. Abū Ḥayyān refers readers to the earlier al-Aʿrāf discussion."}, {"id": "20:71/q11/p2", "position": "With doubled, intensive forms of both verbs.", "reasons": "Bursawī says the first implies an oath and repeated cutting, with the same intensification in crucifying; Ālūsī says doubling intensifies action; Ibn ʿĀshūr takes the forms as manner and forceful nailing, while Asad emphasizes multiple mutilations and crucifixions; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls crucifixion intensified or multiplied."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q12", "question": "What cutting is threatened by مِّنْ خِلَٰفٍ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q12/p1", "position": "Opposite limbs, ordinarily the right hand and left foot, or the reverse.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā, Wāḥidī, Kashshāf, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ṭabrisī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī and Ṭabāṭabāʾī give right hand and left foot. Baghawī allows the reverse; Biqāʿī describes one limb from each side. Ālūsī says this particular pairing follows external explanation, since the verse itself allows other opposite pairings. Abū Ḥayyān calls the act mutilation; Iṣlāḥī views it as punishment for insurgents, displayed publicly."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q13", "question": "How does مِّنْ خِلَٰفٍ work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether min retains its originative or partitive force, or stands in for another preposition.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q13/p1", "position": "Min marks origin or the starting point of cutting, and the phrase is circumstantial: the limbs differ in side.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Rāzī, Samīn and Ibn ʿĀshūr give the circumstantial analysis; Ibn ʿĀshūr compares 7:124 and 5:33. Bursawī distinguishes mere difference from opposition. Ālūsī takes min as partitive or originative, and reports an alternative attachment to an omitted verbal noun, cutting begun from the opposite side."}, {"id": "20:71/q13/p2", "position": "Min may substitute for ʿan or ʿalā, expressing cutting from or on opposite sides.", "reasons": "Ṭabrisī offers both prepositions and treats the phrase as an accusative circumstantial expression. Al-Farrāʾ allows ʿan, ʿalā and bāʾ in such phrases. Ālūsī explicitly rejects Ṭabrisī's substitution analysis."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q14", "question": "Why specify crosswise amputation?", "turns_on": "Whether the specified pattern signals exceptional terror or a known penal practice that avoids disabling or killing the victim outright.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q14/p1", "position": "It makes the threat more dreadful and concrete.", "reasons": "Bursawī says this method heightens terror; Ālūsī reports that some call it the more dreadful method and says the specification gives an assured, definite threat."}, {"id": "20:71/q14/p2", "position": "It follows a customary penal pattern that preserves the use of remaining limbs.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this was apparently the customary mark of criminals rather than a uniquely painful method; he compares the ḥirābah rule in 5:33, which cuts one limb per offense to preserve remaining use. Ālūsī says same-side cutting could kill victims and remove their usefulness."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q15", "question": "What does crucifying فِى جُذُوعِ ٱلنَّخْلِ describe?", "turns_on": "Whether fī is Arabic usage for on, a metaphor of firm enclosure, or a literal account of hollowed trunks.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q15/p1", "position": "Fastening them on palm trunks; fī can mean ʿalā or portray the body as firmly held or enclosed by its support.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Abū ʿUbaydah, Ibn Qutayba, al-Farrāʾ, Ṭabarī, Zajjāj, Wāḥidī, Jishumī, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿĀshūr and others cite Arab usage or poems about al-ʿAbdī, Abū Dhuʾayb, ʿAntara, al-Asadī or Suwayd. Muqātil, Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Farrāʾ compare 52:38; al-Farrāʾ contrasts the body aligned along a trunk with elevation upon it and compares 4:54. Jishumī retains containment as fī's core, and Kashshāf, Rāzī, Bayḍāwī, Nasafī, Biqāʿī and others take a container metaphor; Rāzī calls a bare replacement gloss weak. Wāḥidī al-Wajīz specifies the tops; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says they are tied on trunks rather than mounted like a rider. Bursawī locates the palms along the Nile and defines crucifixion as fastening the back to wood; Ibn ʿĀshūr allows binding or nailing. Burhān says fī is more exact for the middle, whereas ʿalā suggests the top."}, {"id": "20:71/q15/p2", "position": "The trunks were hollowed out and the victims placed literally inside, to die of hunger and thirst.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān and Samīn report the literal account. Ālūsī also reports it but calls it scarcely credible."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q16", "question": "Why specify palm trunks and say 'in' them?", "turns_on": "Whether the choice depicts the position and duration of suffering or suggests ease compared with upward movement.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q16/p1", "position": "The wording stresses height, public visibility, firm confinement and the duration or horror of the punishment.", "reasons": "Nasafī says palms are named for height; Iṣlāḥī says public crucifixion makes an example of them. Biqāʿī says enclosure intensifies horror and deters others; Bursawī says the containment image suggests remaining there a long time. Burhān calls the trunk's middle more exact than its top and reports an image of the trunk as a grave. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies judhūʿ as plural of judhʿ and compares 19:25."}, {"id": "20:71/q16/p2", "position": "Fī suggests the ease of crucifixion, whereas ʿalā would suggest moving upward.", "reasons": "Burhān twice reports this explanation."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q17", "question": "Did Pharaoh carry out the threatened punishment?", "turns_on": "Whether narrative reports can establish an execution that this verse itself only threatens.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q17/p1", "position": "Yes: the magicians were cut, crucified and killed, becoming martyrs.", "reasons": "Al-Suddī reports killing and cutting; Naḥḥās and Qurtubī say the threat was carried out until death. Ibn ʿAbbās says they began the day magicians and ended martyrs after asking for patience and a Muslim death at 7:126. Ālūsī finds the apparent account unobjectionable and says the victory in 28:35 could be victory by proof rather than escape from execution. Rāzī says the Qur'an states only the threat, while reports establish that Pharaoh carried it out."}, {"id": "20:71/q17/p2", "position": "The Qur'an states the threat but does not settle whether Pharaoh carried it out; the reports are not conclusive.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī distinguishes the Quranic account from later reports; Ālūsī reports Rāzī's objection that reports do not establish the event."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q18", "question": "Was Pharaoh the first to use this punishment?", "turns_on": "How much historical weight to give the reports that assign Pharaoh first use.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q18/p1", "position": "Yes, he was the first to cut crosswise or crucify, or both.", "reasons": "Saʿīd says both crosswise amputation and palm-trunk crucifixion; Ṭabarī says Pharaoh first cut in that fashion. Bayḍāwī, Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn Kathīr's Ibn ʿAbbās report, Bursawī and Ālūsī report priority in crucifixion or this punishment."}, {"id": "20:71/q18/p2", "position": "Priority is not established by the reports.", "reasons": "Rāzī's reservation is quoted by Ālūsī, who nevertheless accepts the apparent account."}]}

{"id": "20:71/q20", "question": "How is وَلَتَعْلَمُنَّ أَيُّنَآ أَشَدُّ parsed?", "turns_on": "Whether ayy is an independent interrogative that suspends the verb or a built relative object under the recognition sense of ʿalima.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q20/p1", "position": "Ayyunā is an interrogative subject, ashaddu its predicate; the question suspends the preceding verb's syntactic government.", "reasons": "Zajjāj and Abū Isḥāq say the preceding report cannot govern an interrogative, hence nominative ayyunā. Ṭabrisī says the verb still acts on it semantically. Samīn and Ālūsī say the clause fills two object places if ʿalima means know and one if it means recognize. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the two-person interrogative suspends taʿlamunna. Abū Ḥayyān says the suspended interrogative clause fills two object slots, or one if the verb is construed as 'know'."}, {"id": "20:71/q20/p2", "position": "If ʿalima means recognize, ayyunā may be a built relative object, with an omitted subject before ashaddu in its relative clause.", "reasons": "Samīn compares one analysis of 19:69; Ālūsī attributes the built relative analysis to Sībawayh."}, {"id": "20:71/q20/p3", "position": "Ayyunā is parsed as an object, with its predicate omitted.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān records this as another parse of the clause after 'you will know'."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q21", "question": "What does عَذَابًۭا modify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q21/p1", "position": "It is a tamyīz clarifying 'more severe,' and it is understood with 'more lasting' too.", "reasons": "Ālūsī gives both the expressed and implied scope of the accusative noun."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q22", "question": "What does أَبْقَىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether abqā comes from the ordinary root for permanence or a remote allusion to Pharaoh's gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q22/p1", "position": "More lasting or enduring, especially of punishment.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Farrāʾ, Baghawī, Bayḍāwī and Nasafī give the direct gloss; Ālūsī derives it from baqāʾ, permanence. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys Qur'anic baqāʾ as opposed to perishing and as enduring good with God, including 20:131, 28:60, 42:36, 55:27, 87:17, 16:96, 18:46, 19:76, 21:86, 37:77, 43:28 and 2:248. Her cited Qatāda, Abū ʿUbayda and Rāghib discuss ghābir as remaining: in Lot's punishment, into old age, or like dust left behind; she prefers derivation from remainder or residue. Ṭabrisī's adjacent lexical glosses of īthār, tazkī and zakāt concern choosing and seeking growth or purification, not a competing gloss of abqā."}, {"id": "20:71/q22/p2", "position": "It could allude to gifts that Pharaoh gives favored people.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports this remote alternative, comparing Nimrod's boast, and calls it far-fetched."}]}
{"id": "20:71/q23", "question": "What is Pharaoh trying to achieve with the threats?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:71/q23/p1", "position": "He tries to intimidate the magicians and deter the crowd from their faith, publicly displaying his power.", "reasons": "Rāzī says the threat follows his attempt to discredit them and aims to stop imitators; Qushayrī lists killing, crosswise cutting, crucifixion and severe punishment. Ibn Kathīr says the public execution would make an example; Iṣlāḥī calls it an insurgent's punishment and Kur'an Yolu reports the severe torture threat. Qatāda says the magicians recognized God's sign and prostrated before the threat; Iṣlāḥī says their faith challenged Pharaoh's sovereignty, not merely his religious claim.
